1.title: The Greatest Man of the East
1.context: The book of Job gives no date, king, or location for Uz. Its opening describes Job the way the patriarchs are described: a wealthy household head who offers sacrifices for his own family.
1.question: What does it change for you that the book clears Job of blame before anything happens to him?

1.title: A Father Covering His Children
1.context: Job’s regular burnt offerings for sins his children might have committed in their hearts show a man careful about God long before he is tested.
1.question: What habits of faith do you keep when nothing is wrong?

1.title: The Council and the Challenge
1.context: The scene in heaven is shown to the reader, never to Job. The Hebrew word rendered “Satan” means the adversary or accuser; he appears here among the sons of God presenting themselves before the LORD.
1.question: How do you respond to the idea that Job’s suffering began with a conversation he never heard?

1.title: Four Messengers in One Day
1.context: The disasters arrive in a chain, each messenger interrupting the last, and each is a different kind of loss: raiders, fire, raiders again, and wind. The children die in the final blow.
1.question: Which loss in the sequence strikes you hardest, and why?

1.title: The LORD Gave, and the LORD Has Taken Away
1.context: Job’s tearing of his robe and shaving of his head are mourning customs. His worship, not complaint, is the chapter’s last action, and the narrator clears him of sin in it.
1.question: Have you ever been able to worship God on the worst day? What did that look like?

2.title: He Still Retains His Integrity
2.context: God’s own summary of the first test is that Job retained his integrity and was ruined “without cause,” a phrase that rules out the explanation Job’s friends will spend the book defending.
2.question: What does it mean to hold integrity when there is nothing left to gain by it?

2.title: Skin for Skin
2.context: The second permission again has a limit: Job’s life is spared. The ashes and the pottery shard picture a man sitting in the refuse heap outside the city, scraping diseased skin.
2.question: Where do you go, physically or in your habits, when life reduces you to sitting with loss?

2.title: Curse God and Die
2.context: Job’s wife is the only family member left speaking to him, and her counsel is to end it. Job answers her with a principle he will hold, in harder forms, for the rest of the book.
2.question: When has accepting adversity, not only good, been the hardest part of your faith?

2.title: Three Friends Arrive
2.context: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar come from Teman, Shuah, and Naamah, places outside Israel. Their grief rituals (weeping, torn robes, dust on heads) match Job’s own.
2.question: Who has shown up for you in a crisis before saying anything helpful or unhelpful?

2.title: Seven Days of Silence
2.context: Seven days and nights of mourning echo the period of mourning for the dead. The friends’ silence is widely remembered as their finest hour in the book; everything after it is argument.
2.question: When is sitting with a suffering person in silence better than anything you could say?

3.title: Cursing the Day, Not God
3.context: Job curses his birthday with the language of creation reversed: darkness over light, a day blotted from the year. He never curses God, the one thing both his wife and the accuser expected.
3.question: What do you make of the difference between cursing your circumstances and cursing God?

3.title: Why Did I Not Perish at Birth?
3.context: Job reasons that a stillborn child would never have seen trouble. The speech is lament, not doctrine; the book gives his pain room without correcting it line by line.
3.question: How does honest lament like this fit inside a life of faith, as you understand it?

3.title: Where the Weary Find Rest
3.context: Job pictures death as the one place where the wicked stop raging and slaves are free of masters. The picture says more about his present agony than about any teaching on the afterlife.
3.question: What does Job’s longing for rest tell you about the size of what he is carrying?

3.title: Whom God Has Hedged In
3.context: The hedge Satan mocked as protection (Job 1:10) is now, in Job’s mouth, a wall trapping him in misery. The same word carries both experiences depending on which side of suffering you stand.
3.question: Have you ever felt fenced in by the very God you once felt protected by?

3.title: The Thing I Feared
3.context: Job’s confession that he had feared this all along reframes his careful sacrifices: he lived aware that everything could be taken. His lament ends without rest, ease, or quiet.
3.question: What fear sits underneath your own careful, faithful routines?

4.title: Who, Being Innocent, Has Ever Perished?
4.context: Eliphaz begins graciously, and his question (4:7) is the thesis of the friends’ whole case: suffering of this scale must trace back to sin. The book’s opening chapters exist to test that thesis.
4.question: Where have you heard this reasoning, that bad outcomes prove bad character, in your own life?

4.title: Those Who Plow Iniquity
4.context: Eliphaz appeals to what he has observed in the world: reaping follows sowing. His observation is partial, as Job will answer, but it is sincerely held and ancient.
4.question: When has the “you reap what you sow” explanation been true in your experience, and when has it failed?

4.title: The Night Vision
4.context: Eliphaz’s whispered visitor asks whether a mortal can be more righteous than God. The vision teaches human frailty in general; Eliphaz applies it to Job in particular, which is where the trouble starts.
4.question: How do you tell the difference between a true word in general and a true word for a specific person?

4.title: Great and Unsearchable Things
4.context: Much of Eliphaz’s praise of God here is beautiful and accurate: rain for the earth, help for the lowly, frustration for the crafty. Truth in the abstract is not what Job is disputing.
4.question: Why can accurate teaching still wound when it is aimed at the wrong wound?

4.title: Blessed Is the Man Whom God Corrects
4.context: Eliphaz ends with promises of restoration conditioned on Job accepting correction. The promised blessings are generous; the missing piece is any evidence that correction is what Job needs.
4.question: Have you ever been offered a “way back” that required confessing something you had not done?

5.title: The Arrows of the Almighty
5.context: Job describes his pain as poisoned arrows and arrayed terrors: he experiences his suffering as something God is actively doing, not merely allowing. The friends never take that experience seriously.
5.question: How do you pray honestly when God feels like the source of the pain, not only its witness?

5.title: I Have Not Denied the Words of the Holy One
5.context: Job’s one comfort in asking for death is that he has not denied God’s words. Holding his integrity is the thread he grips through every speech that follows.
5.question: What is the one thing about your own faithfulness you most want to be true at the end?

5.title: As Faithless as Wadis
5.context: A wadi is a desert streambed that runs with meltwater and then dries exactly when travelers need it. Job’s picture of his friends is of help that vanishes at the moment of need.
5.question: Who has been a wadi in your life, and who has been a well? What made the difference?

5.title: Swifter Than a Weaver’s Shuttle
5.context: Job compares his days to a hired laborer’s: hard service, fleeting, and watched. The image of life as breath returns throughout the book and the Psalms.
5.question: How does remembering that life is a breath change what you do with an ordinary day?

5.title: Why Do You Not Pardon My Transgression?
5.context: Job’s question assumes God is watching him constantly (7:17-20) and turns that attention into an indictment: if I have sinned, why no pardon? The book never answers this question directly.
5.question: What question would you ask God first, if you could ask exactly one?

6.title: Does God Pervert Justice?
6.context: Bildad’s explanation of the children’s deaths (8:4) is stated as a deduction from God’s justice: if they died, they must have sinned. The reader, who has read chapters 1 and 2, knows the deduction is wrong.
6.question: How careful are you about explaining other people’s tragedies from the outside?

6.title: We Were Born Yesterday
6.context: Bildad appeals to the tradition of past generations, honestly admitting his own generation knows nothing by comparison. Tradition will prove a weaker authority in this book than experience.
6.question: When has inherited wisdom helped you, and when has it kept you from seeing what was in front of you?

6.title: A Confidence Like a Spider’s Web
6.context: Bildad’s papyrus and spider’s web pictures describe hope without roots. His closing promise, that God will fill Job’s mouth with laughter, is again conditioned on Job being pure and upright on Bildad’s terms.
6.question: What is the difference between hope that is rooted and hope that is just optimism?

6.title: How Can a Mortal Be Righteous Before God?
6.context: Job grants Bildad’s doctrine and raises the practical problem: even a righteous man could not win a hearing. The hymn to God’s power in this chapter includes the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades.
6.question: When have you felt that being right was not enough because no hearing was possible?

6.title: No Mediator Between Us
6.context: Job wishes for a mediator (an arbiter) who could lay a hand on both God and man. Readers across centuries have heard in this wish a longing that the rest of Scripture takes up; the book itself leaves it unanswered.
6.question: What would it mean to you to have someone stand between you and God, with a hand on you both?

7.title: Do Not Condemn Me
7.context: Job’s demand is narrow and specific: show me the charge. He does not yet ask for restoration, health, or his children back; he asks to know why he is being prosecuted.
7.question: What is the question underneath your hardest questions for God?

7.title: Your Hands Shaped Me
7.context: Job argues from craftsmanship: the God who knit him together with such care now destroys the work. The tension between God as maker and God as prosecutor drives the middle of the book.
7.question: How do you hold together God’s care in making you and His allowance of what breaks you?

7.title: A Land Where Even the Light Is Like Darkness
7.context: Job’s description of the grave (Sheol) is the bleakest in this speech: darkness, disorder, no return. Ancient Israel’s picture of the dead was shadowy, and Job pushes it to its darkest edge.
7.question: How do you face the thought of death when you are honest about it?

7.title: God Exacts Less Than Your Iniquity Deserves
7.context: Zophar’s first intervention claims a secret: Job’s punishment is less than he deserves. He offers no evidence, only the height and depth of God’s wisdom compared to Job’s reach.
7.question: Have you ever been told you were getting off easy by someone who did not know your situation?

7.title: You Will Forget Your Misery
7.context: Zophar’s promises (misery forgotten like waters gone by, life brighter than noonday) are conditional in a way Job cannot accept: they require a confession he believes would be a lie.
7.question: What would you refuse to confess, even if confessing promised relief?

8.title: Wisdom Itself Will Die With You
8.context: Job’s tour of God’s reversals (counselors led away barefoot, kings loosened, nations made great and destroyed) undercuts the friends’ tidy system more than any direct rebuttal: God’s governance does not run on their formula.
8.question: Where have you seen God’s ways refuse to fit the formula you were taught?

8.title: Worthless Physicians
8.context: Job accuses the friends of smearing with lies and of arguing God’s case with partiality. His point is sharp: defending God dishonestly is itself a sin against God, a point the epilogue will confirm.
8.question: Why does how we defend the truth matter, and not only whether the truth wins?

8.title: Though He Slay Me
8.context: This is Job’s most famous line of trust inside protest. He expects the hearing may kill him and resolves to hope and to argue in the same breath. Translations differ slightly on the wording; the BSB reads hope.
8.question: What does hope look like when it has no evidence left to stand on?

8.title: Like a Flower, He Comes Forth
8.context: The tree that sprouts again at the scent of water becomes Job’s measure of human hopelessness: a man dies and does not rise until the heavens are no more. The comparison is observation, not revelation.
8.question: How do you live with the nearness of death that this chapter refuses to soften?

8.title: When a Man Dies, Will He Live Again?
8.context: Job wishes God would hide him in Sheol until the anger passed and then remember him. It is a wish, not a claim; the book leaves resurrection as a question Job asks and God’s speeches never take up.
8.question: What do you most hope is true about what comes after death?

9.title: Does a Wise Man Answer With Empty Counsel?
9.context: Eliphaz’s second speech accuses Job of undermining the fear of God itself. The appeal to the gray-haired and aged on “our side” shows the debate hardening into camps.
9.question: When does holding your ground in an argument stop being courage and start being pride, in your own life?

9.title: The Wicked Man Writhes All His Days
9.context: Eliphaz recites the received portrait of the wicked man’s terrors. Job never answers the portrait directly; he answers the application, that it describes him.
9.question: How do you respond when a general truth is pointed at you like a verdict?

9.title: Miserable Comforters Are You All
9.context: Job says he could play their role better than they do: he would encourage and console instead of accusing. The line exposes that the friends’ failure is not intelligence but posture.
9.question: What does the comfort you actually want in suffering teach you about comforting others?

9.title: My Prayer Is Pure
9.context: Job describes God as an attacker (target, archers, poured-out gall) while insisting his own hands are free of violence and his prayer pure. Both claims stand side by side without resolution.
9.question: Can you name a season when you prayed most honestly precisely because you felt attacked by God?

9.title: My Witness Is in Heaven
9.context: Job’s witness and advocate in heaven is a second figure he reaches for, alongside the mediator of chapter 9. Chapter 17 then sinks to his lowest point: Sheol as home, corruption as father.
9.question: Where do you turn when every human witness has stopped believing you?

10.title: The Lamp of the Wicked Is Extinguished
10.context: Bildad’s second speech is a catalogue of traps: net, snare, noose, terror on every side, the king of terrors. It is the doctrine as pure description, with no comfort offered at all.
10.question: When has a description of judgment landed on you as condemnation rather than warning?

10.title: It Is God Who Has Wronged Me
10.context: Job’s counter-claim is the most direct in the book: God has wronged him and closed a net around him. The epilogue’s verdict (42:7) is the place to weigh this sentence, and the book makes the reader wait for it.
10.question: What do you do with prayers and complaints in Scripture that sound almost too bold to say?

10.title: All My Best Friends Despise Me
10.context: The list of abandonments is systematic: family, servants, guests, wife, children, friends. Job’s isolation is total, which is part of why the next paragraph’s hope lands with such force.
10.question: Who stayed, in your loneliest season, and who did not? What did staying look like?

10.title: Chiseled in Stone Forever
10.context: Job wishes his words were inscribed permanently, and in a sense they were: his protest is preserved in Scripture itself. His plea for pity is the first request in the chapter, before the famous declaration.
10.question: What would you want permanently recorded about your hardest season?

10.title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
10.context: The Hebrew word for Redeemer (goel) names a family member who buys back what was lost and vindicates the wronged. Job claims this figure lives and will stand on the earth, and that he will see God in his flesh.
10.question: What does it mean to you that Job’s brightest hope is spoken from his lowest point?

11.title: The Triumph of the Wicked Has Been Brief
11.context: Zophar’s last speech describes sudden ruin for the wicked with vivid disgust. As with Eliphaz, the application to Job is left unspoken and unmistakable.
11.question: Why do you think the friends keep describing the wicked in detail instead of asking Job questions?

11.title: The Wicked Man’s Portion From God
11.context: Zophar charges the generic wicked man with oppressing the poor and seizing houses. In the next episode Eliphaz will aim charges like these at Job by name, without witnesses.
11.question: How do you guard your speech about people whose sins you have inferred rather than seen?

11.title: Look at Me and Be Appalled
11.context: Job asks for the one courtesy left: to be heard to the end before being answered. His terror is not at his losses now but at the evidence of his own eyes about how the world runs.
11.question: When have the facts of the world, as you saw them, frightened you more than your own troubles?

11.title: Why Do the Wicked Live On?
11.context: Job’s counter-evidence is empirical: the wicked grow old in power, die in peace, and say “Leave us alone” to God without consequence. It is the book’s most direct challenge to the friends’ system.
11.question: How do you keep faith honest when the wicked around you are thriving?

11.title: Together They Lie Down in the Dust
11.context: Job’s closing argument of the round is the graveyard: the vigorous and the bitter die alike. The friends’ answers, he says, remain full of falsehood.
11.question: What comfort, if any, do you take from the fact that death levels every difference?

12.title: Is Not Your Wickedness Great?
12.context: Eliphaz opens the third round by denying that God gains anything from Job’s righteousness, then asserts the greatness of Job’s wickedness. The specificity that follows is new, and it is invented.
12.question: What happens to a conversation when one side starts inventing the other side’s sins?

12.title: You Gave No Water to the Weary
12.context: These charges (starved poor, stripped naked, crushed fatherless) appear nowhere in the book’s account of Job’s life, and chapter 31 will answer them point by point. Presenting them as Eliphaz’s accusation, not as fact, matters to the story.
12.question: Have you ever been accused, in detail, of things you did not do? What did proof matter, or not matter?

12.title: The Almighty Will Be Your Gold
12.context: Eliphaz’s closing offer is genuinely warm: reconciliation, restoration, God Himself as Job’s gold. Its warmth depends entirely on the truth of charges Eliphaz cannot support.
12.question: How do you receive good advice that is built on a wrong diagnosis of you?

12.title: When He Has Tested Me, I Will Come Forth as Gold
12.context: Job cannot find God in any direction, yet trusts the outcome of the test he cannot see. The speech holds absence and confidence together without resolving either.
12.question: Where is God hardest for you to find right now, and what do you still trust about the end of the test?

12.title: God Charges No One With Wrongdoing
12.context: Job widens his case from himself to the poor of the whole land: stolen donkeys, naked nights, groaning cities, and no visible judgment. His complaint is about the court’s silence, not only his own file.
12.question: How does concern for others’ unanswered suffering shape your own prayers?

13.title: How Much Less Man, Who Is but a Maggot
13.context: Bildad’s third speech is only six verses, the shortest in the debate, and Zophar never speaks again. The friends’ case is exhausted before Job’s is.
13.question: What do you do when the people arguing with you run out of arguments but not certainty?

13.title: He Hangs the Earth Upon Nothing
13.context: Job’s hymn out-sings Bildad’s: the earth hung on nothing, waters wrapped in clouds, the fringes of God’s ways and a whisper of His power. Job’s theology of God’s greatness is larger than his accusers’.
13.question: How does the scale of creation affect the size of your own case when you bring it to God?

13.title: I Will Maintain My Integrity Until I Die
13.context: Job swears to his integrity and then delivers the friends’ own sermon on the wicked man’s portion himself (27:13-23). He knows their doctrine by heart; he denies its application to him.
13.question: What conviction about yourself would you hold even if every friend told you to drop it?

13.title: Where Can Wisdom Be Found?
13.context: The mining poem celebrates human ingenuity: shafts in forgotten places, mountains overturned, hidden things brought to light. It sets up the question the whole book is asking at a deeper level.
13.question: What can human effort dig up, and what has it never been able to reach in your life?

13.title: The Fear of the Lord, That Is Wisdom
13.context: The poem’s answer is the book’s first description of Job (1:1) returned as a definition: fearing God and turning from evil. Wisdom’s location is known to God alone; man is given its practice.
13.question: How does practicing wisdom differ from possessing answers, in your daily life?

14.title: I Rescued the Poor Who Cried Out
14.context: Job’s memories of the gate are specific and public: the poor rescued, the widow’s heart made to sing, justice worn like a robe. These memories become evidence when Eliphaz’s charges are weighed.
14.question: What do you want to be remembered for doing at the height of your strength?

14.title: Now They Mock Me
14.context: The reversal chapter matches chapter 29 point for point: honor becomes spitting, counsel becomes mockery, answered prayer becomes silence. Job cries out and is merely looked at, he says.
14.question: Which reversal, honor lost or prayer unanswered, would cut you deeper?

14.title: A Covenant With My Eyes
14.context: Job’s oath begins with private purity and includes the rights of his servants, grounded in creation: the same One formed master and servant in the womb. The oath is sworn with self-imposed penalties.
14.question: What standard do you hold yourself to that no one else could enforce?

14.title: My Door Has Been Open to the Traveler
14.context: Point by point, the oath answers Eliphaz’s list from chapter 22: the poor fed, the fatherless defended, gold not trusted, the enemy not cursed, the stranger housed. The book lets the two lists face each other.
14.question: If your life were read aloud as your defense, which lines would you most want read?

14.title: Here Is My Signature
14.context: Job signs his defense like a legal document and asks for the indictment in writing, promising to wear it like a crown. The narrator’s sentence, “Thus conclude the words of Job,” gives his case its formal close.
14.question: What would it take for you to say, with Job, that you had said your whole case and could sign it?

15.title: They Had Failed to Refute Job, and Yet Had Condemned Him
15.context: Elihu son of Barachel appears without introduction beyond his anger. He is angry at Job for justifying himself and at the friends for condemning without refuting, a position no one else in the book takes.
15.question: When have you listened to a long argument and found both sides wrong? What did you do with that?

15.title: The Breath of the Almighty Gives Understanding
15.context: Elihu’s apology for his youth argues that wisdom comes from the Spirit, not age. His wineskin image (full of words, about to burst) is the most self-aware opening of any speech in the book.
15.question: What truth have you had to speak before you felt old enough or qualified enough to say it?

15.title: God Speaks in One Way and in Another
15.context: Elihu claims common ground with Job (both formed from clay) and charges that Job is wrong to say God finds occasions against him. His theme is that God is always speaking; people fail to notice.
15.question: How do you usually notice God speaking, and how might He be speaking in a way you have not noticed?

15.title: One Mediator in a Thousand
15.context: Elihu’s messenger-mediator, who declares what is right and finds a ransom, echoes Job’s own wish in 9:33 in a different key. Elihu applies it through chastening and confession; Job had wanted a hearing.
15.question: What difference does it make to you whether God’s help comes as a hearing or as a rescue?

15.title: Job Speaks Without Knowledge
15.context: Elihu’s second speech restates God’s justice in repayment terms and ends in a verdict on Job: words without knowledge, rebellion added to sin. For all his new angle, his conclusion lands where the friends’ did.
15.question: Where might your newest, sharpest insight still be missing the person in front of you?

16.title: Where Is God My Maker, Who Gives Us Songs in the Night?
16.context: Elihu argues that human righteousness and sin affect other people, not God, and that cries under oppression go unanswered when they never become a cry for God Himself.
16.question: When you cry out under pressure, what are you actually asking for: relief, or God?

16.title: He Grants Justice to the Afflicted
16.context: Elihu’s strongest idea is suffering as instruction: God tells the bound their deeds and opens their ears. It dignifies affliction with purpose, and it still presumes to know what Job’s affliction is for.
16.question: Has suffering ever taught you something prosperity could not? What was the lesson, and its cost?

16.title: God Rescues the Afflicted by Their Affliction
16.context: Elihu warns Job against preferring iniquity to affliction and then lifts his eyes to the rain and clouds. The drift from argument to weather is deliberate: the storm is becoming his Exhibit A.
16.question: What in creation most reliably moves you from argument to awe?

16.title: The Thunder Declares His Presence
16.context: Elihu’s storm theology holds punishment and loving devotion in one system of clouds and lightning. By the end of the chapter the described storm and the real one are hard to tell apart.
16.question: How do you read the weather of your own hard seasons: punishment, care, or something else?

16.title: Stand Still and Consider the Wonders of God
16.context: Elihu’s final charge to Job is the hinge of the book: stop arguing and consider. He does not know that the voice he has been describing is about to speak for itself.
16.question: What would standing still, instead of arguing your case, look like in your situation right now?

17.title: Who Is This Who Obscures My Counsel?
17.context: God answers from the whirlwind, the storm Elihu had been describing, and His first words are a question about Job’s words. The hearing Job demanded opens as a cross-examination.
17.question: What would you expect God’s first sentence to you to be, and how does this one compare?

17.title: Where Were You When I Laid the Foundations of the Earth?
17.context: The morning stars singing and the sea shut behind doors picture a creation ordered and bounded by God alone. Job is asked about his attendance record at events before his birth.
17.question: How does the sheer age and scale of creation change the way you bring your case to God?

17.title: Rain on a Land Where No Man Lives
17.context: God’s survey includes rain spent on empty desert and storehouses of hail for a future war: a world run for purposes wider than human need. No question in the speech concerns Job’s conduct.
17.question: What does it do to your prayers to learn that God does much that is not about you?

17.title: Who Set the Wild Donkey Free?
17.context: The wild animals are presented as free by design, not as resources for man: the donkey scorns the city, the wild ox will not plow. God delights in creatures that refuse domestication.
17.question: What good things in your life refuse to be managed, and might be better for it?

17.title: Does the Eagle Soar at Your Command?
17.context: The ostrich, foolish by God’s own design, still outruns the horse; the war horse laughs at fear. God’s questions end the chapter without a single reference to Job’s case.
17.question: Which of God’s questions in this speech would silence you first?

18.title: I Place My Hand Over My Mouth
18.context: Job’s first reply to God is the shortest speech he makes in the book. The man who filled chapters with argument answers the whirlwind in four sentences and then stops.
18.question: When have you discovered that the right response was fewer words, not better ones?

18.title: Would You Condemn Me to Justify Yourself?
18.context: God names the structure of Job’s complaint exactly: to clear himself, Job has had to condemn God’s government. The offer to let Job run the world’s justice himself is left hanging.
18.question: Where do you catch yourself needing God to be wrong so that you can be right?

18.title: Look at Behemoth
18.context: Behemoth is described in concrete detail (grass, cedar-like tail, bronze bones, lotus shade) and never identified with any known animal by the text itself. Readers have proposed everything from hippopotamus to dinosaur to symbol.
18.question: How do you handle parts of Scripture that resist being pinned to a familiar category?

18.title: Who Is Able to Stand Against Me?
18.context: Leviathan’s introduction is a series of failed human tools: hook, rope, covenant, leash, harpoon. The argument rises from the creature to the Creator in one step.
18.question: What have you tried to manage by technique that could only be faced with humility?

18.title: King Over All the Proud
18.context: The closing description (sealed scales, fiery breath, a seething wake) gives Leviathan the longest portrait of any creature in the book. God presents him without apology, as Job was asked to consider.
18.question: What does it say about God that He describes His most terrifying creature with something like pride?

19.title: Now My Eyes Have Seen You
19.context: Job’s answer quotes God’s questions back and settles on the difference between hearing and seeing. His repentance is “in dust and ashes,” where he has sat since chapter 2.
19.question: What has moved, in your own life, from something you heard about God to something you have seen of Him?

19.title: You Have Not Spoken About Me Accurately
19.context: God’s verdict rebukes the friends’ speaking about Him and vindicates Job’s, twice in one speech. The sacrifice and Job’s intercession are the path back for the men who came to explain God.
19.question: What does it cost, and what does it give, to pray for people whose words hurt you?

19.title: The LORD Restored His Prosperity
19.context: The restoration follows Job’s prayer for his friends, a sequence the text states without comment. The doubled figures match chapter 1 exactly, doubled line by line, except the children, who are the same in number and new.
19.question: Why do you think the livestock are doubled but the children are not?

19.title: Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch
19.context: Job’s daughters are the only children named in the book, and they receive an inheritance among their brothers, unusual enough for the text to record it. His sons go unnamed in both chapters.
19.question: What small, unargued detail at the end of this story stays with you most?

19.title: Old and Full of Years
19.context: Job lives 140 years and sees four generations. The book never tells him, or says he learned, the reason for his suffering; its final interest is the fullness of the life that followed.
19.question: What would it mean to live fully again without ever receiving the explanation you asked for?
